Farnham is a city in the Brome-Missisquoi Regional County Municipality in the Estrie region of Quebec, Canada. It lies on the Yamaska River, near the eastern edge of the Saint Lawrence Lowlands. The city had a population of 10,149 in the 2021 Canadian census.

Permanent Euro-Canadian settlement began around 1800, and the community first developed around water-powered sawmills and flour mills. The arrival of the railway in 1858 changed Farnham into a regional railway and industrial centre. It was the headquarters of the South Eastern Railway and later became an important junction in the Canadian Pacific Railway network.
The present municipality was formed in 2000 through the amalgamation of Farnham and the surrounding municipality of Rainville.
Toponymy

Farnham takes its name from the former Township of Farnham, which was proclaimed in 1798. The township was named for Farnham, Surrey, England. The Commission de toponymie du Québec attributes the choice of name to surveyor and landowner Samuel Gale, who came from that area and was associated with the establishment of the township.
The settlement and its first village municipality were known as West Farnham, or Farnham-Ouest. The shorter name was adopted when it became the Town of Farnham in 1876.
History
Indigenous presence
Farnham is within Ndakina, the ancestral territory of the W8banaki Nation. Ndakina extends westward to the Richelieu River.

Archaeological research in Brome-Missisquoi has documented an Indigenous presence in the region extending back about 5,000 years. A five-year survey conducted in the early 1990s identified 18 pre-contact sites, most of them along the Pike River and others in the Yamaska and Missisquoi watersheds.

The sites show repeated use of the region for hunting, fishing and travel during the Archaic and Woodland periods, as well as trade with communities to the south in present-day New York. By the end of the 16th century, the area formed part of hunting territory used by Western Abenaki groups.
Settlement and municipal development

The Township of Farnham was granted in three sections. Concession A, in the east, was granted to Samuel Gale on October 22, 1798. The central concession went to the heirs of Abraham Cuyler on September 9, 1805, and the western concession to George Allsopp on February 11, 1809.
Permanent Euro-Canadian settlement began near the end of the 1790s. Many of the first settlers were Loyalists or migrants from the United States.

Whipple Cook, an American from Rhode Island, established a sawmill on the south bank of the Yamaska River in 1817. It stood opposite the later Saint-Romuald church, near present-day Conrad-Blain Park. Other sawmills and flour mills followed, and by the 1820s a small settlement had formed around the river crossing.
The West Farnham area had 1,239 inhabitants in 1831. A stagecoach service began passing through the settlement in 1836, and the Farnham post office opened on July 6, 1845.

The first Methodist mission was organized in 1842, and a Wesleyan Methodist church was built in 1844. Anglican services had been held in Cook's Hotel from 1840, the Saint James mission was established in 1847, and its church was erected between 1847 and 1849 on land donated by Colonel James Allsopp.

Roman Catholic services were initially held in private homes. A wooden chapel was completed in 1849 after a brick chapel begun that year was destroyed in a storm. The parish of Saint-Romuald was established in 1851.

Louis Bourdon, a former Patriote who had been deported to Australia after the 1838 rebellion, settled in Farnham in 1849 and opened a general store. He helped organize the West Farnham Bridge Company, which built the first bridge across the Yamaska in 1851.

Bourdon later served as mayor of the parish municipality and became the first mayor of the village municipality of West Farnham when it was incorporated on January 1, 1862. West Farnham became the Town of Farnham on December 28, 1876. Its legal designation changed to city in 1956 and back to town in 1978.
Railway and industrial growth

The Stanstead, Shefford and Chambly Railroad opened its first section at Farnham in 1858, and the first train reached the village on January 1, 1859. The line was extended to Granby that November. In 1871, local investors organized the South Eastern Railway to build a line from Farnham to Newport, Vermont.
The company placed its headquarters in Farnham and built a station, repair shops, a turntable and a large freight yard. The Farnham, Newport line opened on July 9, 1873.

Rail traffic brought workshops, hotels, stores and new residential districts. By 1882, seven tracks left Farnham and more than 18 passenger trains stopped there each day, in addition to freight traffic.
The South Eastern Railway later became part of the Canadian Pacific Railway system, and Farnham remained a junction between east, west and north, south routes.

Mills and the railway were joined by other manufacturers. Industries established in Farnham over time included beet-sugar refining, wood processing, safe manufacturing and textiles. The American textile company Collins & Aikman opened a Canadian plant in Farnham in 1929 to supply the automotive and furniture industries.
The plant remained a large local employer until its closure was announced in 2007, eliminating about 350 jobs.

Fires repeatedly altered the centre of the town. The Saint-Romuald church burned in 1901. A 1909 fire damaged businesses near Depot and Main streets, and another during the night of July 30, 31, 1911 destroyed the town hall, the Wonderland Theatre, hotels, stores and houses.
Firefighters and equipment arrived by rail from Saint-Jean, Sherbrooke and Montreal. The Collège de Farnham burned in 1912 and the hospice in 1916.

The railway station was destroyed by fire during the night of February 8, 9, 1949. Canadian Pacific built the present station in 1950 because Farnham still occupied a strategic point in its network. The repair shops, turntable and express and baggage buildings were removed during the 1960s and 1970s.
The last scheduled passenger train between Montreal and Farnham ran on October 24, 1980.

Farnham and the municipality of Rainville were amalgamated on March 8, 2000. The new municipality took the name City of Farnham and incorporated both the urban centre and the surrounding rural territory.
Military camp

On April 4, 1910, the federal government purchased land west of Farnham for a military training ground. Cavalry units trained there beginning in June of that year. The camp was used during the First World War and closed in 1918. From 1919 to 1940, some of its buildings were used by a Dominion experimental farm.

The site reopened on October 16, 1940, as Camp A, later designated Camp No. It first held civilian internees and refugees sent from the United Kingdom. After closing briefly in early 1942, it housed enemy merchant seamen and then German combatant officers, with a smaller number of other ranks serving as orderlies.

The camp closed again in June 1943 and reopened in September 1944 as an officers' camp. About 2,800 internees, refugees and prisoners of war passed through Farnham before the installation finally closed in 1946.

The training area remains in military use. Candidates from the Canadian Forces Leadership and Recruit School at CFB Saint-Jean deploy to Farnham for field exercises, including Exercise Vimy near the end of basic training.
Geography

Farnham is built on both banks of the Yamaska River at the eastern edge of the Saint Lawrence Lowlands. The urban centre occupies a river crossing near the boundary between the flat agricultural plain to the west and the more broken terrain of the Eastern Townships.

The western part of Brome-Missisquoi, including Farnham, forms part of the Maskoutain plain. Its clay and sand deposits were left by the Champlain Sea after the retreat of the glaciers. Sandy ridges remain near Farnham, including along the corridor followed by Route 235 and Rang Saint-Henri.
The open countryside is used mainly for field crops and livestock farming.

The present territory includes the former municipality of Rainville, which surrounded much of the older town before the 2000 amalgamation. Farnham borders Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville and Saint-Césaire to the north, Ange-Gardien and Brigham to the east, Dunham and Saint-Ignace-de-Stanbridge to the south, and Sainte-Sabine to the southwest.
